name: Zoe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Westmead, the teaching farm attached to the county agricultural college. It's a proper working farm, 250 hectares with 80 dairy cows, 300 ewes and wheat and barley, but every job is also a lesson. I start at half five with milking and two or three apprentices, who are sixteen to nineteen. Then it's fieldwork, lambing or whatever the season says, with students trailing behind me asking why.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when an apprentice who couldn't catch a ewe in September is calving a heifer on her own by spring. What wears me out is the college budget meetings, where people who've never seen a muck heap decide how many staff I get. I use AI now and then to write up apprentice assessments, which saves me an evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the old ways have proved their worth again. In the staff room I'd say we teach the basics properly and add the gadgets that help. I'm not one for posting online, but I'd say it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be content. The college still needs a teaching farm and someone to run it, and my job's as safe as any. The college budget is the only thing that keeps me awake, and that was true long before anybody said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep using the AI for the apprentice write-ups. Yusuf and I would keep putting 150 a month aside, we've got about four months saved. I'd push the college to take on two more apprentices next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to an apprentice who asked whether farming has a future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them yes, and that a good stockperson will always find work. I'd tell them to learn the machines too, but never to stop looking at the animal. That's what I tell them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the budget. Has it been cut before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice in ten years. We lost a shepherd post in 2019 and I've covered it since. If they cut again I'd fight it, but I don't think they'd touch my job.

say: The **old ways** have proved their worth again.
We teach the **basics properly** and add the gadgets that help.
I'd say it **at church**, not online.
think: The college still needs a **teaching farm**, so my job is safe.
Only the **college budget** keeps me awake.
do: Save **150 a month** toward a bigger cushion.
Push the college for **two more apprentices** next year.
S0.quote: The college budget is the only thing that keeps me awake, and that was true long before anybody said AI.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure** because the college needs a working farm.
Her pride centres on **apprentices**, which fits her traditional views.
She is a **moderate AI user**, mainly for paperwork.

steps.text: Keep running Westmead teaching farm and its apprentices as now
Save 150 a month with Yusuf toward a bigger cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming has always changed, and good farmers change with it, carefully. In the staff room I'd say our apprentices need to learn the new software alongside the old skills. At church I'd say look after the young ones who lose their first jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worry is the college, not the farm. If AI can mark and plan lessons, the college might decide it needs fewer lecturers, and a teaching farm is expensive. A college that saves money with software might ask why it still needs 250 hectares and a farm manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other colleges had tried it, I'd bring the farm planning software into the lessons, maybe in the second year. I'd go on the instructors' course to learn it properly. And I'd write a short case to the principal showing what the teaching farm brings in, in fees and milk sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The ground isn't moving yet, but I can hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your apprentices would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, who's 17 and wants to be a farm secretary, doing records and payroll. That's the job software would take first. I'd steer him toward the dairy, where he'd still be needed for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers should change carefully. What does careful mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means watching two or three farms try a thing first, then copying what works. My father did that with the first milking parlour in the valley. He was never first, and he never went bust.

say: Good farmers **change carefully** with the times.
Apprentices should learn **new software** alongside old skills.
We should **look after** the young ones who lose their first jobs.
think: My worry is the **college**, not the farm.
Software savings could make the **teaching farm** look too expensive.
do: Bring **farm planning software** into lessons in year two.
Take the **instructors' course** on the new tools.
Write the principal a **case for the farm** using fees and milk sales.
S1.quote: A college that saves money with software might ask why it still needs 250 hectares and a farm manager.
fieldNote: Her exposure is **institutional**: a college cutting costs.
She cares most about steering **young apprentices** to safer work.
She frames her caution through her **father's example**.

steps.text: Teach farm planning software in lessons from year two
Write the principal a case for the teaching farm's value
Take the instructors' course on farm planning software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast for families and for young people. In the staff room I'd say we must keep training real farmers, whatever happens. At church I'd ask people to pray for the families who lose their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the college would change overnight in 2028, with AI doing the marking, planning and admin. By 2031 robots can milk and lamb, and I'm 63. A teaching farm that teaches young people jobs that robots now do is hard to defend to a college board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd ask the principal for a clear answer on the farm's future to 2031. Yusuf and I would stop the kitchen we were saving for and keep that 12,000 as savings. I'd also look at the college pension and what it pays if I go at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I keep picturing the apprentices' faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for Westmead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be the last years of teaching hands-on farming the old way. The AI takes the paperwork and the planning first, so the farm is cheaper to run for a while. Then robots arrive, and the college has to decide what a farm course even is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we might be living on his building work for a bit, and he's 61 with a bad back. We'd say a prayer and make a plan. Yusuf is better at the praying, I'm better at the plan.

say: It's come **too fast** for families and young people.
We must keep **training real farmers**, whatever happens.
I'd ask church to **pray** for families who lose work.
think: By 2031, a farm teaching **robot-done jobs** is hard to defend.
I'd be **63** with few places to go.
do: Ask the principal for a **clear answer** on the farm to 2031.
Shelve the **new kitchen** and save the 12,000.
S2.quote: A teaching farm that teaches young people jobs that robots now do is hard to defend to a college board.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as the teaching farm's last old-style years.
The household's other earner is **61** with a bad **back**, so the cushion is thin.

steps.text: Ask the college principal about the farm's future to 2031
Shelve the new kitchen and keep the 12,000 saved
Check what the college pension pays at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so let's not waste it. In the staff room I'd say Westmead should become the place local farms learn to run robots. At church I'd say the same thing I always say: look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots come, and I want to retire at 66. If Westmead becomes the place where young farmers learn to manage robots, the teaching farm survives and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once one or two farms nearby have robots working, I'd propose a robot milking unit for teaching, shared with a manufacturer. I'd take the training course myself in 2029. I'd keep saving 150 a month and pay off the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. It feels like a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the apprentices still learn to handle animals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They must. A robot can milk a cow, but someone has to know when she's off her food. I'd keep the sheep hands-on, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the college said no to the robot plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the local farmers' association to back me. If they still said no, I'd stay until 66 and leave them a good plan.

say: Westmead should teach local farms to **run robots**.
think: Five years is **enough** for me, retiring at 66.
A **robot-teaching farm** keeps Westmead and my job alive.
do: Propose a shared **robot milking unit** for teaching.
Keep saving and **pay off the car**.
feel: **Uneasy** but **hopeful**, with a job to do.
S3.quote: If Westmead becomes the place where young farmers learn to manage robots, the teaching farm survives and so do I.
fieldNote: With five years she reframes the teaching farm as a **robot training site**.
She still insists on **hands-on animal skills**.
She'd recruit the **farmers' association** to back her if the college refused.

steps.text: Propose a shared robot milking unit for teaching at Westmead
Take the robot training course herself in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so the college has no excuse. In the staff room I'd say let's design the course for 2035 now. At church I'd say it's in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'll have retired before any of it lands. I'm 68 when the AI arrives and 71 for the robots, and I plan to go at 66. Ten years means my last apprentices learn both the old way and the new way, which is the best of both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Westmead until 66. I'd help design the new robot-era course and train my replacement from 2030. Yusuf and I would save for a small place near Amina and the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, even, to be part of shaping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your replacement to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early milking with the apprentices. That's where you learn whether a youngster is cut out for farming. A robot doesn't need to be up at half five, but a farmer still should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Samir, your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir's in the army, and they'll have robots too, I expect. I'd tell him to come home and learn to farm if he gets tired of it. He won't, but I'd say it.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so the college has no excuse.
We should design the **course for 2035** now.
The future of farming is in **good hands**.
think: I'll have **retired** before any of it lands.
My last apprentices learn **both ways**, old and new.
That's a **good ending** for my working life.
do: Help design the **robot-era course** and train a replacement.
Save for a home **near Amina** and the grandchildren.
S4.quote: Ten years means my last apprentices learn both the old way and the new way, which is the best of both.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **hand over** on her own terms.
Her legacy is the **apprentices**, not the farm itself.
She keeps a strong sense of **farming discipline**: up at half five.

steps.text: Stay as Westmead farm manager until 66

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the college would panic and cut the farm before anyone had a plan. What would help is government money for apprenticeships on real farms, so colleges keep teaching hands-on skills. And honest notice from the college, at least a year, so nobody finds out from a letter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young people. Every September a sixteen-year-old turns up scared of cows, and by spring that apprentice is calving a heifer on her own. I'd like that to still happen in 2040.

headlineQuote: Every September a sixteen-year-old turns up scared of cows, and by spring that apprentice is calving a heifer on her own.
portrait: Zoe, 58, manages a **college teaching farm** with dairy, sheep and cereals.
She trains **apprentices** and uses AI now and then for their assessments.
Her standing worry is the **college budget**, which has cut her team twice.
In the fast scenario she fears the college **closing the farm**; with time she makes it a robot training site.
Traditional and faithful, she backs **apprenticeships** and careful change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the college might close the farm before any plan exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Government money** for apprenticeships on real farms.
